extracted_notes.text: The most prevalent explanation of the anchoring effect is the argument originally made by Tversky and Kahneman, termed anchoring-and-adjusting. Based on this theory, individuals set an anchor according to available information, whether it is provided or individuals already have an anchor in mind, and use this anchor as a point of reference to adjust their answers.
This theory explains inaccuracy in guessing by suggesting that people adjust insufficiently, rendering their final guess closer to the anchors.
This phenomenon was further investigated in other studies and used as an explanation for biases such as hindsight bias and egocentric bias.
Epley and Gilovich found that when anchors are self-generated, people will stop adjusting once they believe they have adjusted their answers to an acceptable range.
Although this process does not guarantee insufficient adjustments, it does result in an answer that is as close to the anchor as possible in the acceptable range.
The simulation theory of empathy suggests that people use their own mental state and reasoning to infer the actions of others.

Aligned with this idea, Tamir and Mitchell found that judgments of the attitude of others are made more quickly for those who are similar to the judge, and greater self-other discrepancy resulted in longer reaction time. In this case, individuals use their own attitudes as an anchor and make adjustments to predict the attitude of others.

cards.card_title: The Power of the First Number

blocks.text_content: Have you ever wondered why a high initial price in a negotiation can influence your perception of value, even if the item is still overpriced? This is the **anchoring effect**, a psychological phenomenon where our minds latch onto a reference point—an *anchor*—to make decisions, often regardless of whether that anchor is actually relevant to the value of the object.

blocks.text_content: Among the various explanations for this behavior, the most influential is the theory of **anchoring-and-adjusting**. But how exactly does this mental process work?

At its core, the theory suggests that we don't just guess randomly. Instead, we establish a starting point based on the information available to us—whether that information was handed to us or something we already knew—and then move away from that point to find a more accurate answer.

The implications of anchoring-and-adjusting extend far beyond simple number guessing. Researchers have used this framework to explain other complex cognitive distortions, where our current perspective acts as an anchor that colors our memory or perception of others.
